pt-PT.question: Segundo as leis de 1845 da Rugby School, o que ganhava uma equipa ao pousar a bola para lá da linha de ensaio?
options: O direito a tentar um pontapé à baliza
pt-PT.explanation: O direito a um «try at goal», uma tentativa de pontapé à baliza: nas leis de 1845 pousar a bola não dava pontos, só os golos marcavam. O ensaio só passou a valer pontos mais tarde, a partir de 1886.

en-US.question: Under the 1845 laws of Rugby School, what did a team earn for grounding the ball beyond the goal line?
options: The right to attempt a kick at goal
en-US.explanation: The right to a «try at goal,» a kick at the goal: under the 1845 laws, grounding the ball scored no points, and only goals counted. A try only became worth points later, starting in 1886.

fontes.titulo: Sports jargon: try - The Irish Times
fontes.excerto: tries were worth nothing when The Laws of Football as Played at Rugby School were drawn up in 1845. The only reward for crossing the line was the resulting opportunity to kick a goal

fontes.titulo: Why is a try called a try in rugby? - Rugby World
fontes.excerto: The word 'try' meant just that. If a team got themselves over the line, they had the chance to try to get points by converting the kick at goal.

fontes.titulo: Scoring down the years (Paul Dobson, Rugby365)
fontes.excerto: In the beginning there were no points in the game as played at Rugby School. The goal counted. Grounding the ball over the opponents' line gave you the opportunity to attempt (try) to improve (convert) the effort into a goal. The try did not count.

In early rugby as played at rugby school, the only scores came from goals and there was no points value associated with scoring. The 1845 rules stated that ... a "TRY at goal" had to be earned by touching the ball down ... 1886 (accepted): ... a try one point.

advogado.notas: Advogado (2.ª passagem): rugbyfootballhistory.com e Rugby World concordam em 1886; sem contradição.
